name: Alabama
catalog_quote: Otherwise, words are usually accented on the last syllable and since this is predictable, final accent is not written.

new_statements.quote: [p. xvi, 1.2] Sometimes vowels in Alabama may have either a high level tone (written as á, í, or ó) or a high falling tone (written à, ì, or ò) and these tones must sometimes be marked for words in the dictionary. For instance, many words for kin or relatives must be written with an accent mark. Otherwise, words are usually accented on the last syllable and since this is predictable, final accent is not written. So, foosi means 'bird' but fósi means 'grandfather'. [p. xiv] Alabama also has 'accent' or 'tone' on certain syllables in a limited number of words where it cannot be predicted by rule, and changes in accent are also used to signal grammatical and semantic differences.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed: final syllable placement (StressTyp2 final stress) as the predictable default and refines it: the 'accent' is a high-pitch/tonal accent rather than dynamic stress, a limited set of words (kin terms etc.) have lexically fixed non-final accent, and morphological grades put high or falling tone on the penult and can suppress the final high tone. The catalog's exceptionless final rule is the default only. The 41-page PDF's text layer is garbled (letter-spaced), so pp. xiii-xiv, xvi, xl-xli were scanned at 300 dpi; the scanned of p. xvi matches the HTML page AlAlphabet.htm verbatim, from which the diacritics in the quote are taken.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is a pitch accent (high level or high falling tone). By default it falls on the final syllable of the word, where it is predictable and left unwritten ('predictable word-final high tone', p. xl). A limited number of words, notably many kin terms, carry an unpredictable (lexical) accent that must be written (foosi 'bird' vs fósi 'grandfather'). Morphological aspect 'grades' add high or falling tone to the penult (or antepenult) of the verb stem; in the L-grade the final syllable then loses its characteristic high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically accented words, especially kin terms (fósi 'grandfather'); on long vowels only the first vowel letter is marked but a level high tone covers the whole syllable and a falling tone falls on the second mora. Grammatical grades (pp. xl-xli): L-grade = high tone on the (lengthened) penult and 'The final syllable lacks its characteristic high tone following the high penultimate syllable accent of the L-grade'; F-grade = high falling tone on the penult 'with predictable word-final high tone remaining (except in negative stems)'; G-, N- and H-grades likewise add high/falling accent to the penult (G-grade also high tone on the antepenult); plural h-infixation adds no accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Sylestine, Hardy & Montler 1993 describe the Alabama of the Alabama-Coushatta Reservation near Livingston, Texas (Introduction / 'About' page); no other dialect is distinguished. Hardy 2005 (not opened) is by the same author and presumably covers the same variety.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the opened source and the catalog on placement: Sylestine, Hardy & Montler 1993 state that words are 'usually accented on the last syllable' and that final accent is predictable, which is the catalog's fixed: final syllable rule. The only tension is one of type: the dictionary calls the prominence 'accent' or 'tone' (high level or high falling pitch, 'high pitch accent' p. xli) and notes a limited set of lexically accented words plus grammatical tone in the aspect grades, so a 'pitch accent' label with default final placement would also be defensible; the catalog's binary final-stress rule is the predictable default, not exceptionless. The listed work (Hardy 2005) could not be opened, so nothing from it can be compared.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in two copies we hold (web alphabet page lines 101-103; printed Intro PDF p. xvi sec. 1.2). (2) The classification 'fixed final' rests on a 1993 dictionary orthography note, but by the language's principal describers, and it is corroborated by the held Gordon 2002 appendix ('Final', via Rand 1968) and by Hardy 2005 pp. 83-84 as paraphrased second-hand; the held Intro's verb-grade section (pp. xl-xli) independently speaks of 'predictable word-final high tone'. Nothing found suggests the classification is wrong. (3) The record's formal quote/cite/loc/grade fields are empty even though the evidence is held and verified — fill them from the held Intro (p. xvi sec. 1.2, plus pp. xl-xli) and grade accordingly; ideally re-read against Hardy 2005 pp. 83-84 when a copy is obtained.
